title: The One With Phoebes Birthday Dinner

jokes.text: It's just spooky, that's all.
jokes.setup: Phoebe says the birthday dinner will have to be Thursday — which is Halloween.
jokes.punchline: Ross's only objection is the vague, childlike complaint that Halloween is 'spooky.'
jokes.explanation: A quick, mild laugh. The joke is in the deliberate inadequacy of 'spooky' as an objection — it's childish and deflating. Competent but not especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Halloween being problematic for dinner plans

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's just spooky.

jokes.text: I'd get mad at him, but I think it's too soon to show my true colors.
jokes.setup: Phoebe says Mike has to work on her birthday — an obvious reason to be upset.
jokes.punchline: Instead of being mad, Phoebe strategically hides her 'true colors' because the relationship is new — an admission of performative niceness that doubles as self-aware relationship comedy.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever line. The phrase 'too soon to show my true colors' is an honest confession of relationship strategy, implying Phoebe is hiding a terrifying inner self. It's sharp, economical, and relatable. Above-average for Friends.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't believe you have to work on my birthday.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I know, I'm sorry. I feel terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you should! But it's okay, I understand. Work is important.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Thank you for being so understanding.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm trying really hard to hide all my crazy right now.

jokes.text: Which one of us should stay with Emma? / Rachel! (simultaneous, emphatic)
jokes.setup: Ross sets up the question of which parent should stay home with Emma.
jokes.punchline: Both point at Rachel simultaneously and immediately, without hesitation — revealing that Ross has zero intention of volunteering.
jokes.explanation: A reliable multi-cam beat — the simultaneous reaction is a classic visual comedy tool. Works well here because the speed of their agreement reveals both characters' self-interest. Solid but familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So who should stay with Emma?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I will!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'll do it!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Me!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can stay with her!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm happy to help!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone just picked Rachel.

jokes.text: Actually, I was thinking maybe both of us could go.
jokes.setup: Both Ross and Rachel named Rachel as the one to stay home.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately pivots to suggesting both go — having just pointed at Rachel, he now wants to abandon the baby too.
jokes.explanation: A quick escalation off the previous joke. Ross's shamelessness is the joke. Works in context but needs the previous beat to function.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's so selfish of them. You know what? I'm gonna get them an extra thoughtful gift.

jokes.text: Thanks. I'll put a lot of extra thought into your gift.
jokes.setup: Ross suggests both he and Rachel abandon baby-sitting duty to attend Phoebe's dinner.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe sarcastically thanks Ross by promising to reciprocate his 'generosity' — implying his gift is about to get much worse.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's passive-aggressive delivery is on-brand and the reversal (gift-giving as punishment) is clean. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe all six of us are finally together!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Monica, Chandler's not here.

jokes.text: What are you talking about? We're together now. / Mon? Chandler's not here. / Oh, dear God.
jokes.setup: Monica enthusiastically celebrates all six friends being together, apparently forgetting Chandler is in Tulsa.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's simple correction ('Chandler's not here') punctures Monica's enthusiasm. Monica's 'Oh, dear God' is a perfect deflation — she's so wrapped up in the moment she forgot her own husband.
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, dear God' is a perfectly proportionate reaction — Monica's horror at forgetting Chandler is funnier than any elaborate joke would be. The structure is tight and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Where's Chandler? He was supposed to be here!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's missing! He could be anywhere! He could be dead! Oh God, he's dead!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait... he texted me. He's at the store.

jokes.text: Is it true the reason you're in Tulsa is, you fell asleep in a meeting and took the job without realizing what you were saying yes to?
jokes.setup: Chandler opens his new Tulsa team meeting professionally.
jokes.punchline: His subordinate Ken immediately asks point-blank whether the urban legend about Chandler accidentally taking the job is true — exposing his humiliating backstory to his new team.
jokes.explanation: Lands well because it's so brazen — a subordinate asking the boss the most embarrassing possible question in a first meeting. Chandler's situation (accidentally moving to Tulsa) is a recurring comedic premise handled sharply here.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? No! I was very much awake during that meeting. I heard everything they said.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Yes. I fell asleep, and when I woke up, someone was shaking my shoulder, and I just said 'yes' to whatever they were asking. I'm a statistical analysis and data reconfiguration.

jokes.text: Well, don't believe everything you hear, Ken. But yeah, that's true.
jokes.setup: Chandler begins with the standard deflection ('don't believe everything you hear').
jokes.punchline: He immediately confirms the story anyway, undercutting his own authority before the meeting has started.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler moment. The setup-to-deflation is fast and clean. 'But yeah, that's true' destroys the pretense of authority with zero ambiguity. His resigned self-awareness is his defining comedic trait.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Claudia, you can't smoke in here.

dialogue.speaker: Claudia
dialogue.line: Why not? I'm just blowing smoke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, blow it outside.

jokes.text: Claudia, aren't you supposed to blow smoke up the boss's ass?
jokes.setup: Chandler's employee is literally smoking in the office. He comments on it.
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses the idiom 'blow smoke up the boss's ass' (meaning flattery) which now has a literal double meaning — she IS literally blowing smoke, in the direction of her boss.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever wordplay. The idiom perfectly collides with the literal situation. It's the kind of double-meaning joke that rewards the audience. Well above average for a multi-cam sitcom of this era.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Does a guy who looks like Joey eat?

jokes.text: Right now I can't remember why. [I quit smoking]
jokes.setup: Chandler explains he used to smoke but quit.
jokes.punchline: Surrounded by smoking coworkers, he 'can't remember' his reason for quitting — implying the temptation is overwhelming his memory.
jokes.explanation: A reliable joke with a clear situational irony. Chandler's self-delusion is well-deployed. Functional and character-appropriate but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: Your wife can't monitor your smoking if she's in New York.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's true.

jokes.text: Would you like one? / Would Joey like two pizzas?
jokes.setup: An employee offers Chandler a cigarette.
jokes.punchline: Chandler answers the question about whether he wants a cigarette by rhetorically asking whether Joey would want two pizzas — invoking Joey's legendary appetite as a universal 'yes' benchmark.
jokes.explanation: A cute internal reference that characterizes both Chandler (self-aware about his weakness) and Joey (defined by his appetite). Works especially well for fans who know Joey. The rhetorical structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I was going to go as a sexy nurse, but then I realized I'd have to shave my legs, so I went with a sexy cat instead.

jokes.text: You know, it's almost rude that I'm not smoking.
jokes.setup: Everyone in the meeting is now smoking, and Chandler is the odd one out.
jokes.punchline: Chandler rationalizes his desire to smoke by framing abstinence as a social faux pas — the most absurd possible justification.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's escalating rationalization is delivered with perfect commitment. The inversion — turning a vice into a social obligation — is clever and very specific to his neurotic, over-justifying personality. A highlight of the Tulsa subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I could watch!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, I could... leave. I could leave and watch TV in the other room.

jokes.text: No, I can't. I can't smoke. If I smoke, my wife would kill me. / I'm sorry, but isn't your wife back in New York? / I've always liked you, Ken.
jokes.setup: Chandler invokes Monica's wrath as his reason not to smoke — his wife as an authority figure.
jokes.punchline: Ken points out that Monica is in New York — i.e., she can't actually enforce anything. Chandler's delighted 'I've always liked you, Ken' signals he's going to smoke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The three-beat structure is flawless: (1) Chandler's Monica-fear excuse, (2) Ken's logical loophole, (3) Chandler's immediate capitulation framed as affection. 'I've always liked you, Ken' is a great quotable line. The joke perfectly dramatizes Chandler's Monica dynamic while giving him an enabling sidekick. Approaches the 8-anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You don't wanna watch?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. I was just being polite anyway.

jokes.text: I've always liked you, Ken.
jokes.setup: Ken has just pointed out that Monica isn't there to enforce the no-smoking rule.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's affectionate response implies he appreciates Ken enabling his bad behavior — a deadpan acknowledgment of his own weakness.
jokes.explanation: Four words doing a lot of work. The understatement is perfect — Chandler doesn't say 'you're right, I'll smoke,' he just warmly endorses the person who gave him permission. Economy score is near-perfect; nothing wasted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, you guys are gonna be great parents. And Monica, you're gonna be an amazing mom. And Chandler, you're gonna be an amazing dad. And I'm gonna be the cool uncle who gives them really inappropriate gifts and teaches them all the stuff you don't want them to know.

jokes.text: Hey. / And 'treat' it is. [Monica in a sexy Halloween costume at the door]
jokes.setup: Trick-or-treaters appear at Monica and Chandler's door.
jokes.punchline: Monica answers in a revealing/sexy Halloween costume, and the joke is in the contrast between the wholesome trick-or-treat moment and Monica's outfit — 'treat' becomes a double entendre.
jokes.explanation: A reliable but not especially creative gag. The 'sexy Halloween costume answers trick-or-treaters' setup is familiar. The double entendre of 'treat' is light. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Did you know that in Hawaii, cigarettes are called 'happiness sticks'? It's true. I read it somewhere. Very popular there. The natives have been using that term for centuries.

jokes.text: Wow. So glad I changed. I almost wore my threadbare robe that can't contain my breasts.
jokes.setup: Monica is dressed provocatively for ovulation sex with Chandler.
jokes.punchline: She notes with faux-relief that she changed, implying her 'casual' alternative (a robe that 'can't contain' her breasts) would have been equally or more inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: Funny in its specificity — 'threadbare robe that can't contain my breasts' is a vivid, ridiculous image. Monica's obliviousness to social norms is well-characterized here.

jokes.text: This is not what I'm wearing. I'm ovulating and Chandler's gonna be home. So I thought we would try before dinner.
jokes.setup: Phoebe arrives expecting to walk over to dinner together.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately overshares her ovulation-driven sex plan with no filter, treating it as completely normal conversation.
jokes.explanation: Monica's total lack of social filter around her baby-making efforts is a solid recurring bit. The casualness with which she explains her sex schedule to Phoebe is funny. Standard Friends cringe-lite.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you want to come to the bedroom?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No thanks, I'm good. Maybe later with a biscuit.

jokes.text: Unless, I mean, if it helps, I could stay and watch. / No! / Well, I didn't want to anyway. You know, just thought I'd be polite and offer.
jokes.setup: Monica explains she and Chandler need privacy for ovulation sex.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe offers to stay and watch as a gesture of 'politeness' — a completely surreal inversion of social norms, delivered with earnest sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A great Phoebe joke. The offer to watch as a gesture of politeness is classically Phoebe — she operates on a completely different social logic from everyone else, delivered with total sincerity. The follow-up ('Well, I didn't want to anyway') doubling down on the etiquette framing is excellent. High character integration — only Phoebe does this.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't tonight, I have a headache.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You had a headache yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's a really persistent headache.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Plus, I think I'm coming down with something. And my back hurts. And I just remembered I have to alphabetize my socks.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Your socks are already alphabetized!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: By COLOR! I need them organized by thread count. And also, I just found out I might have been in a plane crash. A small one. Nobody died, but I was definitely on that plane. I'm very shaken up about it.

jokes.text: Okay. See you there. Happy humping.
jokes.setup: Phoebe leaves Monica and Chandler to their ovulation sex appointment.
jokes.punchline: 'Happy humping' as a farewell — Phoebe's complete comfort with saying this as a cheerful send-off.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Two words that are hilariously inappropriate as a farewell, delivered as if wishing someone a safe trip. Very quotable, very Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, I found cigarettes in your jacket. You promised you quit!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, it was just one cigarette. I bummed it off Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Just one? Then what about these other packs?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Alright, fine. Maybe it was a few cigarettes. Like... a pack.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A pack, Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, two packs. But that's it! That's all I bought!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And the rest?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three cartons. I bought three cartons. But I was stressed!

jokes.text: My God, don't people know you're not allowed to smoke in public spaces?
jokes.setup: Chandler has just been smoking in a Tulsa office (after being enabled by Ken). He smells of smoke.
jokes.punchline: He self-righteously complains about smoking in public spaces — completely ignorant that he is the smoker causing the problem.
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony — the audience knows what Chandler is oblivious to. His sanctimony is well-deployed and the hypocrisy is immediately obvious. A clean situational joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, hello, she's my daughter. Of course I don't want to leave her. But come on, I'm not gonna lie to you guys - I really, really don't want to go to Barbados.

jokes.text: Actually, in Oklahoma smoking's legal in offices with fewer than 15 people.
jokes.setup: Joey (or Phoebe) reacts to Chandler smelling of smoke.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately deploys the specific Oklahoma smoking law trivia — the same justification used in the Tulsa meeting — revealing he used this rationalization to smoke.
jokes.explanation: Works beautifully as a callback — the specific legal trivia he absorbed at the meeting is now his personal excuse. The recontextualization makes it funnier than the original use.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, my mom was great with kids! And you know what? Baby Monica was ugly.

jokes.text: Oh, you smoked. / No. I just happen to know a lot of trivia about smoking in different states.
jokes.setup: Phoebe correctly deduces Chandler has been smoking from his quoting of Oklahoma law.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's alibi — that he merely has encyclopedic trivia about smoking laws by state — is transparently absurd.
jokes.explanation: The alibi is a great comic invention — the specificity of 'I know trivia about smoking laws in different states' is so implausible it's funny. Well-structured with a clear setup/punchline. Chandler's desperation is vivid.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You should totally go out tonight, Rachel. You know, let loose, have some fun.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, I don't know...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Come on, it'll be da bomb! You'll be all like, 'Fo' shizzle, my nizzle!' That's what the kids are saying these days.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I'm down with the kids. I'm totally phat and fly. Word to your mother!

jokes.text: For example, in Hawaii, cigarettes are called lei-lana-lukus.
jokes.setup: Chandler is doubling down on the claim that he just knows smoking trivia.
jokes.punchline: He invents a completely fake Hawaiian term for cigarettes — 'lei-lana-lukus' — which sounds like nonsense Hawaiian-ish syllables and is transparently fabricated.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny escalation. The fake word sounds just plausible enough to be funny, and Chandler's confidence in delivering a completely invented fact is perfect. The absurdist specificity elevates this above a standard cover-story joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That is so phat!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, stop. Just stop. Nobody says that anymore. You sound like my dad trying to be cool at a school assembly.

jokes.text: Are you kidding? That woman has the nose of a bloodhound.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks 'Do you think Monica will smell it?' (the cigarette smoke).
jokes.punchline: Phoebe invokes Monica's superhuman sense of smell — an established character trait — to underscore that Chandler is definitely caught.
jokes.explanation: Functional character-based joke. Monica's controlling perfectionism extends to sensory awareness. 'Nose of a bloodhound' is a bit of a cliché but works in context.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? My slang is cool. I'm down with the kids. I'm hip, I'm with it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: How you doin'? All that and a bag of chips! Fo' shizzle!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm the king of slangy! The sultan of cool! The czar of... of... phat!

jokes.text: And the breasts of a Greek goddess.
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes Monica as having 'the nose of a bloodhound.'
jokes.punchline: Joey seamlessly extends the animal/mythological metaphor to comment on Monica's breasts — a completely non-sequitur addition that is entirely on-brand for Joey.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's addition is perfectly timed, perfectly economical, and could only be Joey. The parallel structure ('nose of a bloodhound / breasts of a Greek goddess') makes it sound almost poetic. The non-sequitur breast compliment for his friend's wife is simultaneously inappropriate and sweetly sincere — pure Joey. Approaches the 8-anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, I forgot my keys!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh come on, Rachel!

jokes.text: Oven cleaner. [Chandler's attempt to cover the smoke smell]
jokes.setup: Chandler needs to cover the cigarette smell before Monica gets home. He grabs something from under the sink.
jokes.punchline: He chooses oven cleaner — a caustic industrial chemical — as his cologne replacement. The visual of Chandler spraying oven cleaner on himself is absurd.
jokes.explanation: The escalating desperation of Chandler's cover-up choices is well-paced. 'Oven cleaner' is a great specific bad choice — it implies he's willing to chemically burn himself rather than face Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We're locked out! Oh, fiddlesticks! Great Caesar's ghost! Jumping Jehoshaphat!

jokes.text: Unscented. [The oven cleaner is unscented]
jokes.setup: Chandler has grabbed oven cleaner to mask smoke smell.
jokes.punchline: The oven cleaner is unscented — meaning his terrible plan fails on its own terms. He's going to smell like chemicals AND smoke.
jokes.explanation: One word. That's the whole joke. 'Unscented' as a single-word punchline delivered after the oven-cleaner beat is a masterclass in comedic economy. The reveal that his desperate plan is also completely ineffective is perfectly timed. Strong candidate for best single-word joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I haven't eaten anything all day.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: All day? Phoebe, I had one lunch and I'm starving!

jokes.text: Welcome home. I've missed you. / You want to join me in the bedroom? / No, thanks, I'm good.
jokes.setup: Monica has set up a seductive homecoming — candles, lingerie, an invitation to the bedroom.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, committed to his shower cover story, declines the bedroom invitation with the casual 'No, thanks, I'm good' — a response so wrongheaded it's funny.
jokes.explanation: The 'no thanks, I'm good' response to a seduction attempt is funny in its wrongheadedness. Chandler choosing to maintain the shower ruse over responding to Monica's seduction is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Will the rest of your party be joining us?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not sure. You see, my friends are of a rather pedestrian disposition, whereas I myself am a woman of considerable refinement and erudition. So I shall dine alone this evening, as is befitting someone of my intellectual stature.

jokes.text: ...I soiled myself during some turbulence.
jokes.setup: Chandler needs an excuse to take a shower (to wash off the smoke smell). He claims he 'feels gross.'
jokes.punchline: When Monica pushes, he escalates to: 'The truth is, I soiled myself during some turbulence.' — a spectacularly embarrassing excuse that is somehow worse than admitting to smoking.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection and escalation. Chandler would rather confess to soiling himself on a plane than admit to smoking — which reveals exactly how terrified he is of Monica. 'Soiled myself during some turbulence' is a great comic phrase: specific, vivid, and completely humiliating. Strong laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I would like to formally request the utilization of more sophisticated vernacular in our subsequent discourse.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Furthermore, I find it incumbent upon myself to elevate the lexicon to such heights of erudition that comprehension becomes virtually unattainable for those of pedestrian intellectual capacity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: One might even postulate that the juxtaposition of such grandiose phraseology with my intrinsic persona creates a paradoxical tableau of magnificently ludicrous proportions.

jokes.text: What do I smell? I smell smoke. / Did you smoke? / Yes. But I just had one. / Two. / Two tiny cigarettes. Okay, five. / A pack. Two pack-- A carton. / Three big fat cartons in two days!
jokes.setup: Monica smells the cigarette smoke on Chandler despite his attempts to cover it.
jokes.punchline: The escalating confession sequence: Chandler's numbers keep climbing under Monica's interrogation — from 'one' to 'two' to 'five' to 'a pack' to 'a carton' to 'three big fat cartons in two days.' Each beat gets a bigger laugh.
jokes.explanation: The best comedic sequence in the episode. The escalating confession is a textbook example of multi-cam escalation comedy — each step up the scale gets a bigger laugh, and 'three big fat cartons in two days' is a perfect peak. The structure is impeccable: each revelation tops the last while Monica's silence forces the next confession. Chandler's inability to stop confessing is pure character comedy. Comparable in structure quality to the best Friends moments.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, but we do need this table. Do you have any idea how many people are waiting?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I would suggest that you take your impatience and your rusty sword and go back to the Renaissance Fair from whence you came, you medieval wench.

jokes.text: She is? / Yeah. / What about Monica? / You only hear Monica's side of that. Okay, that little fatso was a terror!
jokes.setup: Ross reassures Rachel that his mom is great with kids.
jokes.punchline: Rachel brings up Monica as a data point. Ross immediately dismisses 'Monica's side' and calls young Monica 'that little fatso' — revealing a sibling perspective on Monica that is delightfully unsympathetic.
jokes.explanation: Ross's sibling dismissal of fat Monica is on-brand and genuinely funny. 'That little fatso was a terror' is a great line — the affectionate contempt in 'little fatso' is specific and character-rich. Monica's former weight is a recurring Friends gag, but the sibling framing gives it fresh energy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, did you see that commercial where the guy coughs up his lung? I literally cannot watch that anymore.

jokes.text: You need to learn some new slang.
jokes.setup: Ross is enthusiastically encouraging Rachel to go out using outdated expressions: 'your oyster,' 'kick up your heels,' 'paint the town red.'
jokes.punchline: Rachel flatly tells him he needs new slang — a simple but accurate puncturing of Ross's dad-energy.
jokes.explanation: Light but effective. The joke is in Rachel's flat delivery of an obvious truth. Not particularly original but well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You have no willpower.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from someone who eats pizza like it's a sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I do not!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You fold it in half and eat it like a taco.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's the correct way to eat pizza!

jokes.text: No, no! You know what? You're not getting back in there! The baby's fine. Now, scram! / Yeah, hit the bricks! Tell your story walking!
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to push Rachel out the door so she'll stop hovering over Emma.
jokes.punchline: Ross's tough-guy encouragement escalates from 'scram' to 'hit the bricks' to 'tell your story walking' — an escalating series of old-timey gangster expressions that undercut his authority.
jokes.explanation: Ross trying to be tough while using hopelessly dated slang is a good character moment. 'Tell your story walking' is especially funny because it's such a non-threatening old-man threat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what just happened? Did we break up? Are we getting a divorce? Should I call a lawyer? Because I'm pretty sure I can't afford a lawyer. Oh God, I can't even afford a decent sandwich right now.

jokes.text: I was just going to say that I left my keys.
jokes.setup: Ross has just delivered an elaborate tough-guy speech pushing Rachel out the door, culminating in 'Tell your story walking!'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's mundane, deflating response — she just needed her keys — makes Ross's whole performance completely ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. The structure is excellent — the more elaborate Ross's speech, the funnier the mundane reveal. Rachel's flat delivery of 'I was just going to say that I left my keys' completely destroys Ross's moment. Great economy, clean structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Fine, okay, I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ugh, really? That's so gross.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do it again.

jokes.text: Holy moley, are we in a pickle now!
jokes.setup: Ross is locked out of the apartment after pushing Rachel out.
jokes.punchline: His instinctive exclamation is 'Holy moley, are we in a pickle now!' — a Ned Flanders-level G-rated expression of panic that reveals his true unhip self.
jokes.explanation: 'Holy moley, are we in a pickle now' is a great character-specific expression — immediately after trying to be tough with 'hit the bricks,' Ross reverts to this hilariously square exclamation. The character whiplash is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Just knock the door down!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't knock the door down. I'm not strong enough. I'm like a girl.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hey!

jokes.text: I knew we were coming here tonight. I ate nothing all day. / What about me? I only had one lunch today.
jokes.setup: Phoebe complains about being starving at the restaurant while waiting for the late party.
jokes.punchline: Joey one-ups her suffering: he 'only had one lunch today' — revealing that his baseline is multiple lunches, so having just one is a genuine hardship for him.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'I only had one lunch today' is exquisitely Joey — it only works because we know his standard is multiple lunches. The delivery of genuine grievance about having 'only' one lunch reveals his entire character in five words. High quotability, high character integration. Very close to the 8-anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what if the baby falls off the changing table?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, the baby's not even born yet.

jokes.text: Their arrival is in the offing.
jokes.setup: The maitre d' asks if the rest of their party is coming. Joey says 'Yes, they are expected presently.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe adds 'Their arrival is in the offing' — inexplicably speaking in formal Downton Abbey-style language, escalating Joey's attempt at sophistication to an absurd degree.
jokes.explanation: The gradual escalation of formal language from Joey and Phoebe as they try to impress/appease the maitre d' is a fun bit. 'In the offing' is an appropriately obscure choice for Phoebe to reach for.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, did I leave the stove on?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, you don't cook.

jokes.text: Perhaps you'd— — No, they're coming. We're waiting right here. Joseph! One needn't worry. They shan't be long.
jokes.setup: The waiter suggests they take a smaller table.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe escalates to even more archaic formality — 'one needn't worry,' 'they shan't be long' — now speaking as if she's a Victorian aristocrat.
jokes.explanation: Escalation of the previous archaic language bit. 'They shan't be long' is a good escalation. The character commits to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What if he gets sick? What if he falls? What if he chokes?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, he's not going to choke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You don't know that!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What if a plane crashes through the apartment? What if we're attacked by a swarm of bees? What if a meteor hits the building?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What if the sun explodes?

jokes.text: Oh, one really does have a stick up one's ass, doesn't one?
jokes.setup: The maitre d' (speaking in third person / formal register) pressures Phoebe and Joey about giving up the large table.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe turns his formal register against him — using his own 'one' construction to deliver a rude insult ('stick up one's ass') in his own stilted voice.
jokes.explanation: The best single line of the episode. The joke is structurally perfect: Phoebe mirrors the maitre d's formal register (the 'one' construction) and deploys it to deliver a supremely rude insult that lands with surprising elegance. The juxtaposition of formal grammar and vulgar content is brilliantly executed. The fact that Phoebe uses his own linguistic weapon against him is a joy. Comparable to the 8-anchor benchmark — genuinely exceptional for a multi-cam sitcom.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Have you not seen that ad? Where the little kid walks through Grandpa? It's chilling!
jokes.setup: Monica lectures Chandler about how smoking is bad for him in 'this day and age.'
jokes.punchline: She references a specific anti-smoking ad where 'the little kid walks through Grandpa' — a horrifying image that Monica describes as 'chilling' with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Monica's sincere investment in a terrifying anti-smoking ad is a funny specific detail. 'The little kid walks through Grandpa' is a genuinely disturbing image that she describes earnestly, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: We can't order until your whole party arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How long is that gonna be?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: I don't know, sir.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, can I at least eat the rolls that are already on the table?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What about the stuff that's already been eaten? Can I finish that?

jokes.text: Willpower? I've watched home movies of you eating Ding Dongs without taking the tinfoil off!
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Chandler's willpower in resisting cigarettes, implying she has strong willpower.
jokes.punchline: Chandler deploys the ultimate hypocrisy card: he's seen video evidence of Monica eating Ding Dongs without removing the tinfoil — a spectacle of compulsive food behavior that destroys her moral authority.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The specificity of 'eating Ding Dongs without taking the tinfoil off' is perfect — it's a vivid, grotesque image that invokes fat Monica, home video evidence, and Monica's compulsive eating all at once. Chandler's deployment of this as a willpower counter-argument is brilliant. 'You said that was sexy!' makes it even better. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't leave! If I go to the bathroom, Phoebe's gonna be sitting here alone and the table's gonna get taken!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So what are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm saying... you gotta hold the table. Or I'm not drinking any more water.

jokes.text: You said that was sexy!
jokes.setup: Chandler has described Monica eating Ding Dongs through tinfoil in home movies.
jokes.punchline: Monica's defense is that Chandler told her it was sexy — which suggests Chandler once found this disgusting behavior attractive, implicating him in her compulsion.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag to the Ding Dongs joke. Monica turns the revelation back on Chandler — he was complicit. The image of Chandler seductively telling Monica that eating tinfoil-wrapped Ding Dongs is sexy is absurd and hilarious. Five words that maximize the previous joke. Near the top of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'll move! I'll move! Don't touch me!

jokes.text: That's right, because I forbid you to smoke again. / You forbid me? / I've flown a long way to see my loving wife. Is she here, by the way?
jokes.setup: Monica declares she 'forbids' Chandler to smoke — asserting control.
jokes.punchline: Chandler questions 'you forbid me?' and then sarcastically asks if his 'loving wife' is around — implying the monster he's speaking to isn't her.
jokes.explanation: 'Is she here, by the way?' is a great line — Chandler asking if his loving wife is present while his terrifying wife is right in front of him. Well-deployed character dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: You guys need to stop being so disruptive.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We're not being disruptive!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm so hungry I could drink olive oil.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Sir, please don't drink the olive oil.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Too late.

jokes.text: Is this the most upset you could be? / I think so. / Well, then I might as well... do this. [Lights a cigarette in front of Monica]
jokes.setup: Monica declares she is 'very, very upset' about the smoking.
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks if this is her peak upset — confirming she can't get angrier — then immediately lights a cigarette in front of her, as if he's found a loophole.
jokes.explanation: Smart comedic logic — Chandler's 'max upset is already hit, so I have nothing to lose' reasoning is both absurd and character-consistent. His impish refusal to back down when cornered is a good Chandler moment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know, Chandler, if you're having trouble with the whole conception thing, maybe you should try taking your clothes off a little faster.

jokes.text: So you're going to put out that cigarette, we're gonna put this fight on hold, and go have sex. / Fine. What? / What, do you have cigarettes in your ears? Sex!
jokes.setup: Monica announces a plan mid-fight: table the argument and have ovulation sex.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's confused 'Fine. What?' gets the response 'What, do you have cigarettes in your ears?' — Monica's exasperated insult weaponizing the cigarette as a metaphor for his poor listening.
jokes.explanation: 'Do you have cigarettes in your ears?' is a fun specific insult that ties back to the smoking subplot. Monica's ability to weaponize any available material is on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe you want to have sex right now. We just came from my uncle's funeral.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm feeling very alive right now.

jokes.text: All right, fine, I'll do it, but no talking! / And no cuddling. / And no kissing your neck. / Oh, good! I hate it when you do that! [beat] And lots of kissing your neck!
jokes.setup: Chandler reluctantly agrees to ovulation sex but sets conditions (no talking, no cuddling).
jokes.punchline: Monica joins in with her own condition: no kissing her neck. Chandler agrees — 'Oh, good! I hate it when you do that!' — then immediately reverses: 'And lots of kissing your neck!' revealing his enthusiasm overtaking his grudge.
jokes.explanation: The setup-misdirection-reversal is clean and funny. Chandler's smug 'Oh, good! I hate it when you do that!' followed immediately by 'And lots of kissing your neck!' shows his resolve crumbling in real-time. The speed of the reversal is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm never smoking again. I promise.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, I'm just promising to hide it better.

jokes.text: I would, but I bruise like a peach.
jokes.setup: Rachel demands Ross knock down the apartment door to rescue the baby.
jokes.punchline: Ross's excuse for not breaking down the door: 'I bruise like a peach' — a delicate, non-masculine explanation that is completely Ross.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. 'I bruise like a peach' is perfectly Ross — physically delicate, oddly specific, and delivered with matter-of-fact seriousness. The fruit metaphor applied to a grown man's physical fragility is a great comic image. High quotability. Near the 8-anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: When Ross was little, he was very confused about gender. He wanted to wear dresses and play with dolls.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mom!

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: What? It was adorable! He looked like a little girl.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Can we please not do this right now?

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Oh, come on, it was just a phase.

jokes.text: What if she jumps out of the bassinet? / Can't hold her head up, but jumped.
jokes.setup: Rachel catastrophizes about Emma jumping out of the bassinet.
jokes.punchline: Ross's dry correction: a baby who can't hold her own head up is unlikely to have executed a standing jump.
jokes.explanation: Ross's flat, logical takedown of Rachel's anxiety is well-executed. The economy of 'Can't hold her head up, but jumped' is excellent — it dismantles Rachel's panic with minimal words.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: It was easier to leave your father.

jokes.text: Listen. / What? What? / A pigeon. No. No, wait, no. An eagle flew in! Landed on the stove and caught fire! The baby, seeing this, jumps across the apartment to the mighty bird's aid. The eagle, however, misconstrues this as an act of aggression and grabs the baby in its talon. Meanwhile, the faucet fills the apartment with water. Baby and bird, still ablaze, are locked in a death grip, swirling around the whirlpool that fills the apartment!
jokes.setup: Rachel has been catastrophizing about all the things that could go wrong with Emma alone — bird flying in, stove on, water running. Ross has been dismissing each one.
jokes.punchline: Ross takes all of Rachel's separate anxieties and weaves them into an increasingly insane narrative — a burning eagle, a heroic baby, a death-grip whirlpool — that escalates to a completely surreal disaster movie.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's high points. Ross takes Rachel's separate paranoid scenarios and builds them into an escalating absurdist narrative with its own internal logic (the eagle 'misconstrues' the baby's heroism). The structure is excellent — each element from Rachel's earlier fears is incorporated. The commitment to the narrative ('the mighty bird's aid') elevates it. Approaches the 8-anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You've been using sex to manipulate me this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. It works, doesn't it?

jokes.text: Boy, are you gonna be sorry if that's true.
jokes.setup: Ross has just described the elaborate eagle/baby/whirlpool disaster scenario.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat response acknowledges the absurdity while maintaining her anxiety — she can't entirely dismiss the scenario.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to Ross's absurdist monologue. Rachel's inability to fully dismiss the scenario — 'Boy, are you gonna be sorry if that's true' — is funny because it reveals her anxiety is so deep that even a burning eagle seems possible. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'll have the meatball sub, extra meatballs, and... actually, you know what? Give me two meatball subs. No, three. Three meatball subs!

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Sir, that's a lot of food.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You think I'm not gonna finish this? I'm Joey Tribbiani. I can eat anything. Bring it on!

jokes.text: Well, how about this? Another table leaves, right, but there's still some food left on their plates. Okay, what's the restaurant's policy about people eating that?
jokes.setup: Joey and Phoebe are starving at the restaurant and can't order. The maitre d' says they can't hold the table much longer.
jokes.punchline: Joey's solution to hunger: inquire about the etiquette of eating other guests' leftovers.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey. The idea that he's seriously inquiring about the protocol for eating strangers' leftovers — framed as a reasonable business question — is perfectly in character. 'What's the restaurant's policy about people eating that?' is a great line because it treats scavenging as an etiquette issue.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey, you keep calling me that and I really don't like it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Bitch?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes! Stop it!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh come on, bitch, I'm just messing with you.

jokes.text: It's frowned upon. / But it happens.
jokes.setup: Joey has asked about eating other guests' leftovers.
jokes.punchline: The maitre d' says it's 'frowned upon.' Joey immediately follows with 'But it happens' — not as a joke, but as a sincere confirmation that this is a real thing he has witnessed or done.
jokes.explanation: Three words that are funnier than most full jokes. 'But it happens' implies Joey has personal experience with the practice and finds the maitre d's framing as 'frowned upon' insufficient to deter him. The deadpan economy is extraordinary.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We got stuck in traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, it was terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Is it edible?

jokes.text: All right, I got to go to the bathroom. / You can't go. / No, no, no. I can't hold this table on my own. If they ask me to move, I'll cave. / Well, if you ask me to stay, I'll pee.
jokes.setup: Joey needs to go to the bathroom but Phoebe insists he can't leave her alone to defend the table.
jokes.punchline: Joey's counter: 'If you ask me to stay, I'll pee' — a perfectly proportionate escalation that makes his biological need as important as the table crisis.
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure of the exchange ('if they ask me to move, I'll cave / if you ask me to stay, I'll pee') is clean and funny. Joey's declaration is delivered with the seriousness of a negotiating position.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm okay, I'm okay. She's just deciding. There's nothing wrong with that. I'm okay, I'm okay.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm gonna hurt somebody.

jokes.text: Miss? Miss? / Okay, fine, I'll move. All right. You don't have to manhandle me.
jokes.setup: Left alone at the table, Phoebe is being pressured by the maitre d' to give up the large table.
jokes.punchline: Despite her earlier bravado, Phoebe immediately caves — the maitre d' doesn't even need to use force, just call 'Miss?' repeatedly — and she complains about being 'manhandled' when presumably nothing physical has happened.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's immediate capitulation despite the elaborate setup confirms what Joey already said — she'll cave. The 'manhandled' complaint is a good exaggeration. Solid character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm so hungry I can barely stand up.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, me too.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, you're hungry too? I thought you were just weak from... whatever.

jokes.text: Will you stop staring at us now? / That depends. Will your friend stop drinking olive oil directly from the bottle? / Probably not.
jokes.setup: Phoebe challenges the maitre d'/waiter for staring at them after they've been relocated.
jokes.punchline: The waiter reveals Joey has been drinking olive oil directly from the bottle at the table — an act so bizarre it justifies the staring. Phoebe's 'Probably not' accepts this without embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The reveal that Joey is drinking olive oil from the bottle while Phoebe is trying to maintain dignity is a perfect visual gag that also maximally characterizes Joey. Phoebe's resigned 'Probably not' — accepting Joey's behavior as an unchangeable fact of life — is pitch-perfect. The structure (challenge/reveal/acceptance) is clean and the image is both absurd and entirely credible. Comparable to the 8-anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I would never lie to someone just to sleep with them. That's morally reprehensible.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? What about the time you told that girl you were JFK Jr.?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That was different!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How is that different?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because... because I believed it at the time!

jokes.text: What is taking you so long? Come on, let's get it over with! / In a minute, sweet cakes. / Spend more time with the tie! That will make a baby.
jokes.setup: Monica is waiting impatiently for Chandler to get ready for ovulation sex.
jokes.punchline: Chandler is fussing with his tie — an absurd priority — and Monica's sarcastic 'Spend more time with the tie! That will make a baby' punctures his dithering.
jokes.explanation: 'Spend more time with the tie! That will make a baby' is a good sarcastic line. The absurdity of Chandler prioritizing his appearance for scheduled sex is a good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll have the chicken, and for the lady, I'll have the manipulative shrew.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, that's not on the menu? Then I'll have the same thing.

jokes.text: Oh, sure. Now you're Mr. Sensitivity. But when you wanted to have sex after my uncle's funeral-- / That was a celebration of life!
jokes.setup: Chandler says he can't make love when they're fighting — invoking sensitivity.
jokes.punchline: Monica throws back that he was willing to have sex after her uncle's funeral. Chandler's unapologetic defense: 'That was a celebration of life!' — reframing funeral sex as a noble act.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. 'That was a celebration of life!' delivered with complete sincerity and moral confidence is a perfect Chandler line. The dark premise (funeral sex) is reframed in the most positively earnest possible way. The economy and conviction make this land hard. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, what did you order?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A manipulative shrew.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's not on the menu.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, what is that?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: I think he means the cobb salad.

jokes.text: And if I do, I promise I will hide it so much better from you.
jokes.setup: Chandler promises he won't smoke again. Monica says 'Really?'
jokes.punchline: He adds the caveat: 'And if I do, I promise I will hide it so much better from you' — a confession that his real failure was poor concealment, not smoking itself.
jokes.explanation: A great Chandler line. The honesty of promising to hide future transgressions better — rather than promising not to commit them — is a perfect character revelation. The structure builds beautifully: sincere-sounding promise, then the reveal that his actual takeaway is better deception. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, I have a great embarrassing story about Ross from when he was a kid.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Oh no, we've all heard that one already.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really? Which one?

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: All of them.

jokes.text: One time I was about to leave Ross to go to the beauty parlor. And he got so upset he took off all his clothes, tucked his willy between his legs, and cried out, 'Mommy, I'm a girl. Take me with you.'
jokes.setup: Judy Geller is trying to comfort Rachel about separation anxiety, saying it gets easier over time.
jokes.punchline: She illustrates with a childhood story about Ross — specifically that he expressed separation anxiety by tucking his genitalia between his legs and impersonating a girl to manipulate his mother.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most surprising jokes. The specificity and darkness of the image — a young Ross performing a full gender transformation as a manipulation tactic — is both horrifying and hilarious. 'Tucked his willy between his legs' is a perfect phrase (using a childish word for maximum incongruity). The mother recounting this story casually to comfort Rachel is brilliant. Dark, specific, and character-rich — this is exceptional multi-cam comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? I was just trying to help!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, you ordered for everyone without asking.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I know what you all like!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not the point. You need to let people decide for themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Fine! Chandler, control me. Pretend I'm not even here.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wish I could.

jokes.text: Somehow, over time, it got easier to be apart from you. [Ross to Rachel, in context of the willy story]
jokes.setup: Judy has just told Rachel the mortifying story of young Ross tucking his willy between his legs.
jokes.punchline: Ross's response to his mother is the deadpan 'Somehow, over time, it got easier to be apart from you' — a simultaneously wounded and funny acknowledgment of the story's damage.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button. Ross's line works on multiple levels: it's a comeback to his mother, an acknowledgment that she traumatized him into independence, and a commentary on the absurdity of the story. The deadpan delivery of genuine psychological damage is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, where is Emma's other sock? I laid out two socks this morning!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, it's just a sock.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Just a sock?! Monica, Emma needs both socks! What if her foot gets cold? What if she develops a complex about asymmetrical clothing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I think the sock fairy took it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This is NOT funny! My daughter is out there with one sock and everyone's just sitting around like it's NORMAL!

jokes.text: You are welcome.
jokes.setup: Ross has said 'Somehow, over time, it got easier to be apart from you' — clearly a wound, not gratitude.
jokes.punchline: Judy takes his comment as a compliment and says 'You are welcome' — either oblivious to the sarcasm or choosing to embrace it.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly delivered. Judy's 'You are welcome' as a response to Ross's wounded deadpan is a great tag — it completes the joke chain and reveals her imperviousness to guilt. The economy is impeccable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm sorry I yelled about the dinner disasters.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Do you think my anger made things worse?

jokes.text: I am still so mad at you for smoking! / But you said you forgave me. / It was just a couple of cigarettes, no big deal. / I was ovulating and you said you wouldn't have sex if we were fighting. / You tricked me to get me into bed? / That's right. I got mine.
jokes.setup: Monica has apparently forgiven Chandler for the smoking. He reminds her of this.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals she was lying about forgiving him — she used faux-forgiveness to get Chandler into bed during her peak ovulation window. 'That's right. I got mine.'
jokes.explanation: 'That's right. I got mine' is a spectacular line — Monica's unapologetic, almost triumphant confession that she manipulated Chandler for sex is both villainous and deeply funny. The reversal (Chandler was the one being tricked) is well-constructed. High character integration — Monica's ruthless pragmatism is perfectly depicted.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's it! I'm done! I'm leaving and never coming back!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh wait, hold on, my phone's ringing.

jokes.text: I feel so used.
jokes.setup: Monica has confessed she tricked Chandler into having sex with her.
jokes.punchline: Chandler — a man — expresses feeling 'used' after being manipulated into consensual sex with his wife, inverting the typical gender dynamic of this complaint.
jokes.explanation: Four words, great inversion. Chandler's earnest sense of victimhood at being tricked into sex is a good gender-role subversion. The sincerity makes it funnier than a knowing wink would.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're ovulating?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, and apparently I'm very desperate. So desperate that I'm willing to have sex with Smokey the Bear.

jokes.text: Waiter? All right, this is gonna go fast, so try to keep up. Risotto with shaved truffles and the rib steak with the golden chanterelles and the Bordelaise sauce, unless any of that stuff I just said means 'snails.'
jokes.setup: Joey and Phoebe are finally allowed to order after waiting over an hour. Joey approaches this with military urgency.
jokes.punchline: Joey orders with authority — until the caveat 'unless any of that stuff I just said means snails' — revealing his sophisticated-sounding order is a performance; he has no idea what any of it means.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. Joey confidently ordering high-end food by name and then revealing he has no idea what any of it means — but his line in the sand is 'snails' — is a perfect character joke. The contrast between his confident delivery and his cluelessness is maximally funny. 'Unless any of that stuff I just said means snails' is a great quotable line. Approaches the top of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I feel like I'm being used for sex. I'm like a pretty girl.

jokes.text: Oh, well they're both exquisite-- / Both it is. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Joey asks which pasta the waiter recommends.
jokes.punchline: The waiter begins to deliberate ('they're both exquisite') and Joey immediately interrupts: 'Both it is.' He orders both pastas without waiting for a recommendation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey food logic. He asks for a recommendation not to choose between them but to confirm he should order both. 'Both it is' treats the waiter's superlative as a mandate for maximum ordering. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I would never abandon my friends. I'm loyal. I'm like a dog.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm leaving now.

jokes.text: Now, let's go, baby. It's food time. Bring it, bitch.
jokes.setup: Joey has finished ordering an enormous amount of food.
jokes.punchline: He sends the waiter off with 'Now, let's go, baby. It's food time. Bring it, bitch' — treating the waiter like a corner-man before a boxing match, with 'bitch' used as a term of camaraderie.
jokes.explanation: Extremely quotable. Joey's relationship with food is so intense he speaks to waiters the way fighters speak to their coaches. 'Bring it, bitch' is funny because it's simultaneously aggressive and affectionate — Joey isn't being rude, he's being motivational. Very high quotability and character integration. One of the most memorable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We should take Emma home.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Oh, just one more minute. We're having so much fun!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mom, you've had like five margaritas.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So? You're babysitting!

jokes.text: I'll wait to put your order in. / What did I ever do to you? / Nothing, bitch.
jokes.setup: Joey has just called the waiter 'bitch.' The waiter retaliates by saying he'll delay putting the order in.
jokes.punchline: Joey asks 'What did I ever do to you?' — genuinely confused about what he did wrong. The waiter mirrors his language back: 'Nothing, bitch.' Joey has created a monster.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback. The waiter adopting Joey's own language ('Nothing, bitch') is a great comedic reversal — Joey's attempt at motivational trash-talk has infected the waiter, who now uses it as a weapon. Joey's oblivious question 'What did I ever do to you?' shows he still doesn't connect the dots. Great structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So, Kennedy had sexual experience?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: My ex-boyfriend dated Kennedy's niece.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, which ex-boyfriend? Because if it's Fun Bobby, that doesn't count.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, it was Richard.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Richard dated Kennedy's niece? How is that not the first thing you tell people?

jokes.text: You guys are over an hour late. / What happened to you two? / So sorry. / We got locked out of the apartment. / That's a great story. Can I eat it?
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel arrive an hour late with their excuse.
jokes.punchline: Joey's response to 'we got locked out of the apartment' is 'That's a great story. Can I eat it?' — his hunger is so consuming that he judges all information by whether it's edible.
jokes.explanation: 'Can I eat it?' as a response to an excuse is one of the best Joey jokes in the episode. The logic is perfect: Joey is so hungry that he has reduced all incoming information to the binary question of edibility. High character integration, extraordinary economy. Among the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not sharing this food with anyone. This is all for me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Watch and learn, people. This is how a professional eats.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're witnessing greatness right now.

jokes.text: I know what you mean, this menu's incredible. — Ross bruises like a peach. He bruises like a peach.
jokes.setup: Phoebe sympathizes about the overwhelming menu.
jokes.punchline: Joey's response — 'Ross bruises like a peach' — is a callback to the locked-out scene that Joey clearly cannot stop thinking about, delivered as if it's relevant commentary on the menu.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that also reveals Joey has been silently obsessing over Ross's peach-bruising admission. The non-sequitur delivery in context of a menu discussion is what makes it funny — Joey is clearly stuck on that detail.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: How was everything?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, it was great! The manipulative shrew was delicious!

jokes.text: I would never lie to get someone into bed. / You used to tell girls you were a Kennedy.
jokes.setup: Chandler is offended that Monica tricked him into bed, claiming he would never lie to get sex.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately calls him out: 'You used to tell girls you were a Kennedy.' — a devastating, specific historical fact about Chandler's past.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. The specificity of 'you used to tell girls you were a Kennedy' is perfect — it's such a specific, delusional, ambitious lie that it's immediately hilarious. Ross's immediate, matter-of-fact delivery of this information destroys Chandler's moral high ground. Extremely quotable. Near the top of the episode's quality range.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know what you're thinking. 'How can he be happy?' Well, I'll tell you how. I got a table, I got food, and I got nobody telling me to stop eating. This is the best birthday ever!

jokes.text: A little tight, isn't it? Why didn't you get a bigger table? / You had a big table but they made you move. / Shut up, Monica.
jokes.setup: The whole group is now crammed at a small table after Phoebe and Joey were forced to downsize.
jokes.punchline: Monica helpfully explains they had a bigger table but were made to move — exposing the humiliation. Phoebe's 'Shut up, Monica' is a perfect, tired response to being reminded of her defeat.
jokes.explanation: A good payoff to the table subplot. 'Shut up, Monica' is a perfect weary response. Functional callback comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, well, I suppose that Chandler will have the smoked duck. / And I suppose that Monica will have the manipulative shrew.
jokes.setup: The waiter makes a pointed joke about Chandler's smoking history ('smoked duck').
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately retaliates by ordering 'the manipulative shrew' for Monica — a dish that doesn't exist but perfectly describes her.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's crown jewels. The waiter's setup ('smoked duck') is good but Chandler's immediate pivot to 'the manipulative shrew' for Monica is exceptional — it's a callback to the fight, a vicious insult, AND a fake menu item, all in four words. The structure is perfect: waiter dishes, Chandler retaliates with equal wit. Very quotable, very high character integration. Among the top 3 jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: And I suppose that Monica will have the manipulative shrew.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just made a pointed comment about Chandler having the smoked duck.
jokes.punchline: Chandler fires back that Monica will have the 'manipulative shrew' — a fake menu item that doubles as an insult, calling out Monica's trickery from earlier.
jokes.explanation: The best single-line joke in the episode. It operates on three levels simultaneously: (1) it mirrors the smoked duck structure, keeping the menu format; (2) it invents a fake dish that is a devastating character insult ('manipulative shrew'); (3) it's a callback to Monica's revelation that she tricked Chandler into sex. The word 'shrew' is specifically chosen — it's both insulting and archaic enough to feel like a dish name. Perfect structure, extraordinary character integration, and extreme economy. This is the joke the whole Monica/Chandler arc of the episode builds to.

jokes.text: How did I miss that? [The waiter, to himself]
jokes.setup: Chandler has just ordered 'the manipulative shrew' for Monica.
jokes.punchline: The waiter's self-critical 'How did I miss that?' — expressing genuine regret that he didn't come up with that joke himself.
jokes.explanation: A great button on the manipulative shrew joke. The waiter breaking character to regret not landing that joke himself is a funny meta-moment. His professional pride in wordplay makes him a surprisingly funny minor character.

jokes.text: I'll give you another minute. / What, where you going? / He said she wanted the shrew!
jokes.setup: The waiter says he'll give them another minute after the shrew joke disrupts ordering.
jokes.punchline: Joey calls after him, insisting on order completion — 'He said she wanted the shrew!' — treating 'the manipulative shrew' as a real menu item that must be properly recorded.
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious insistence that 'the shrew' is a real order is a perfect extension. His priority is getting everyone's food ordered, not understanding the joke. The callback gives him the last word on the manipulative shrew bit in a funny way.

jokes.text: You ever hear the story about when Ross' mom went to the beauty salon? / You mean the willy story? / They already know it.
jokes.setup: Rachel is about to repeat Judy's willy story to change the subject.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's immediate recognition ('You mean the willy story?') and Ross's defeated 'They already know it' establishes this as an instantly-canonical embarrassment — the story has already spread.
jokes.explanation: A great running gag beat. The speed with which 'the willy story' becomes the common name for the incident — and Ross's tired 'They already know it' — shows how permanently damaging the story is. Good economy.

jokes.text: Chandler, control your woman.
jokes.setup: Monica has ordered for everyone without consulting them. Phoebe complains.
jokes.punchline: Ross tells Chandler to 'control your woman' — an outrageously outdated, chauvinistic phrase that is funny precisely because (a) it's Ross saying it and (b) no one has ever controlled Monica in the history of this show.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurdity of the suggestion — controlling Monica is the most impossible task in the Friends universe. Ross's casual deployment of an archaic phrase is on-brand for his sometimes-clueless character. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: She dropped her sock. [Rachel, spotting Emma across the restaurant]
jokes.setup: Ross is about to make a toast to Phoebe. The birthday dinner is finally coming together.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's attention immediately snaps to Emma dropping a sock — she cannot stop obsessively monitoring the baby even from across the restaurant.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. The timing — interrupting Ross's birthday toast — is well-constructed. Rachel's compulsive baby-monitoring is the episode's secondary comic throughline.

jokes.text: She still has not noticed that the baby's sock is on the ground. / It's a good toast.
jokes.setup: Rachel is panicking about Emma's dropped sock while Ross's toast goes undelivered.
jokes.punchline: Joey, completely ignoring the sock crisis, comments on Ross's toast — 'It's a good toast' — despite the fact that the toast has not been given and nothing has been said.
jokes.explanation: Joey pre-emptively evaluating a toast that hasn't been given is very funny. It suggests he's been anxiously waiting for the toast — and food — for so long that he's grading things prospectively.

jokes.text: She still has not noticed that the baby's sock is on the ground.
jokes.setup: Judy is supposedly watching Emma but hasn't noticed the sock.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's dry observation — delivered as if she's a nature documentary narrator — highlights the absurdity of the babysitting situation.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational joke that works as a bridge to the escalating sock-attention crisis. Phoebe's detached commentary is in character.

jokes.text: Oh, for God's sake, Judy, pick up the sock! Pick up the sock! Pick up the sock!
jokes.setup: Rachel has been unable to get Judy's attention about the baby's dropped sock.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe erupts at the birthday dinner — screaming 'Pick up the sock!' at Judy across the restaurant — finally breaking on her birthday.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe snapping at the birthday dinner is a good payoff to the evening's mounting frustrations. The repetition of 'Pick up the sock' is an effective escalation. The delivery would land big in a studio audience.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, was that rude? Did my little outburst blunt the hideousness that is this evening?
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just screamed across the restaurant at Judy about the sock.
jokes.punchline: She immediately follows with mock-politeness: 'I'm sorry, was that rude?' and then the reveal of her genuine feelings: 'the hideousness that is this evening' — a savage indictment of her own birthday party.
jokes.explanation: 'The hideousness that is this evening' is a great phrase — it has the cadence of literary damnation applied to a sitcom birthday dinner. Phoebe's oscillation between faux-politeness and genuine rage is well-written.

jokes.text: Pheebs, I don't think that's us. / Oh, well, this is-- This is not over! Hello?
jokes.setup: Phoebe's phone rings mid-speech and she answers it, apparently still ranting.
jokes.punchline: Ross points out the ringing phone isn't for her — she's been yelling into a phone call she didn't make, then continues the rant into the actual call.
jokes.explanation: A cute physical comedy beat — Phoebe's rant interrupted by a fortuitously timed phone call that turns out to be Mike. The confusion about whose phone is ringing is a reliable multi-cam device.

jokes.text: "We"? / There are some adult willy stories they don't know.
jokes.setup: Ross says 'we should've been stronger' (about leaving Emma at home). Rachel says 'we?'
jokes.punchline: Judy threatens: 'There are some adult willy stories they don't know' — implying a cache of additional mortifying Ross stories that she can deploy as leverage.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. The implication that there is a whole repertoire of 'adult willy stories' — plural, more explicit — is a perfect escalation of the earlier joke. Judy weaponizing her son's humiliation as a conversational negotiating tool is delightfully dark. 'Adult willy stories' is a great phrase.

jokes.text: Well, you see, I'm ovulating. / Oh, yeah, that's what she says. / Maybe you're not ovulating. Maybe it's a clever ruse to get me into bed. / Yeah, Smokey, that's what it was. I just can't get enough.
jokes.setup: Monica explains the fight to others at the table, mentioning ovulation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, still suspicious, theorizes Monica faked the ovulation to seduce him. Monica's sarcastic 'Yeah, Smokey, that's what it was. I just can't get enough' perfectly deflates his self-flattery.
jokes.explanation: 'Yeah, Smokey, that's what it was' is a great put-down. The 'Smokey' nickname (referencing his smoking) is an efficient callback, and the sarcasm of 'I just can't get enough' perfectly mocks his vanity.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah, that's what she says. — Maybe you're not ovulating. Maybe it's a clever ruse to get me into bed. — Yeah, Smokey, that's what it was. I just can't get enough.
jokes.setup: Monica reveals to the table she was ovulating; Chandler is still processing the trick.
jokes.punchline: Chandler suggests it was all a ruse; Monica's withering response — 'Yeah, Smokey, that's what it was. I just can't get enough.' — sarcastically implies she is so consumed by desire for Chandler that she devised an elaborate scheme, while the nickname 'Smokey' is a callback to his smoking.
jokes.explanation: Monica's sarcasm is sharp — the idea that she 'just can't get enough' of Chandler is delivered as an obvious absurdity. The nickname 'Smokey' as a pointed callback to his smoking while also slightly emasculating is clever double-duty writing.

jokes.text: She tricked me into having sex with her. / So? You got to have sex, right? / What's the matter with me? Why am I such a girl?
jokes.setup: Chandler complains to Joey that Monica tricked him into sex.
jokes.punchline: Joey's pragmatic 'So? You got to have sex, right?' — cutting through Chandler's wounded dignity to the obvious fact — leads to Chandler's self-aware lament: 'What's the matter with me? Why am I such a girl?'
jokes.explanation: A great exchange. Joey's 'So? You got to have sex, right?' is the perfect masculine pragmatist response to Chandler's grievance, and Chandler's 'Why am I such a girl?' — while dated in its framing — lands as genuine self-awareness. The character contrast between Joey's simple worldview and Chandler's emotional complexity is well-executed.

jokes.text: Okay, I'm gonna take off. / What? / I love you guys too, but Mike got off work early. / Wait. / I'm not the-- I'm not the kind of girl that just ditches her friends to be with her boyfriend. You know what? I am. / Bye, guys. Judy! Bye.
jokes.setup: Everyone has just apologized to Phoebe and promised to be fully present for her birthday.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately announces she's leaving for Mike — mid-birthday — after everyone sacrificed for her. Her self-correction ('I'm not the— I'm not the kind of girl...You know what? I am.') is the perfect admission.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structural highlights. The irony is perfect — after the whole episode of friends being late to her party, Phoebe ditches her own birthday the moment Mike is available. 'You know what? I am' as a self-correction is a great Phoebe moment: honest, unapologetic, perfectly in character. Great structural payoff.

jokes.text: If Phoebe's gone, can we take Emma home? / That's a good idea. Our babysitter just pounded another chardonnay.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has left her own birthday dinner. Rachel sees an escape opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Ross agrees, adding that their babysitter 'just pounded another chardonnay' — establishing that Judy Geller, sitting at the bar with the infant, is visibly drunk.
jokes.explanation: 'Our babysitter just pounded another chardonnay' is a great line — the realization that their emergency backup plan (Judy) has been drinking at the bar while watching the infant is a dark comedy escalation. 'Pounded' is exactly the right word.

jokes.text: If Phoebe's gone, can we take Emma home? — That's a good idea. Our babysitter just pounded another chardonnay.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just left; Rachel immediately pivots to going home to Emma.
jokes.punchline: Ross agrees, citing that their babysitter (Judy) has just had another chardonnay — revealing Judy has been drinking at the bar while babysitting, which is both alarming and funny.
jokes.explanation: 'Pounded another chardonnay' is a great word choice — 'pounded' implies speed and volume. The implication that Judy has been drinking while watching Emma is a dark note delivered lightly.

jokes.text: So, I'm probably still ovulating. Do you want to give it another try? / All right.
jokes.setup: Everyone is leaving. Monica and Chandler are alone.
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'I'm probably still ovulating' as a dinner table come-on — treating their earlier manipulative sex encounter as a simple, repeatable activity — and Chandler's weary 'All right' agreeing.
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the ovulation subplot. Chandler's resigned 'All right' is good — he's given up all resistance. Light but appropriate for the episode's coda.

jokes.text: So, I'm probably still ovulating. Do you want to give it another try?
jokes.setup: Everyone has left; Chandler and Monica are alone at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately pivots back to baby-making — the fight, the dinner, the evening all secondary to the ovulation window.
jokes.explanation: In-character capstone to the ovulation subplot. The 'probably' is a funny qualifier — she's not even sure, but it's worth trying. Monica's relentlessness about conception is consistent.

jokes.text: So, you've never had sex with a Kennedy, have you? / Actually, Richard was a Kennedy on his mother's side. / Why did you break up with that guy?
jokes.setup: Chandler was accused of claiming to be a Kennedy to pick up girls.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals that her ex-boyfriend Richard Burke is actually a Kennedy on his mother's side — which Chandler finds inexplicably appealing ('Why did you break up with that guy?').
jokes.explanation: A great callback with an unexpected twist. Monica's revelation about Richard being a Kennedy (on his mother's side — a suitably thin connection) recontextualizes the Kennedy joke from earlier. Chandler's 'Why did you break up with that guy?' shows his Kennedy-awe overcoming his jealousy of Richard. Good character work and clean callback structure.

jokes.text: Why did you break up with that guy?
jokes.setup: Monica has just revealed Richard had a Kennedy connection.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response — wondering why she broke up with the man connected to American royalty — reveals his own insecurity while being funny in its directness.
jokes.explanation: Good beat on the Kennedy reveal. Chandler questioning the break-up reveals his own insecurity about Richard while also being an absurd non-sequitur. Short and punchy.
